Standard Text: Explain the political contributions of Benjamin Franklin to the U.S., including the "Join or Die" cartoon and Albany Plan of Union.
Cartoon Title: Join, or Die
Creator: Benjamin Franklin
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Benjamin Franklin, "Join, or Die," Pennsylvania Gazette, 1754. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A segmented snake divided into eight labeled pieces representing the colonies, with the caption 'JOIN, or DIE.'
Fit / Note: The standard explicitly names the 'Join or Die' cartoon and the Albany Plan of Union; America's first political cartoon.

Standard Text:
Analyze the social, political, and economic causes of the events and groups of the American Revolution, including:
• The Quartering Act, 1765
• The Stamp Act, 1765
• The Declaratory Act, 1766
• The Townshend Acts, 1767
• The Boston Massacre, 1770
• The Boston Tea Party, 1773
• Intolerable/Coercive Acts, 1774
• Sons of Liberty
Cartoon Title: The Able Doctor, or America Swallowing the Bitter Draught
Creator: Attributed to Paul Revere (after London Magazine engraving)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Able Doctor, or America Swallowing the Bitter Draught," 1774. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: British ministers force tea down the throat of a woman (America) held down on the ground, symbolizing the Coercive Acts and Boston Port Act.
Fit / Note: Directly illustrates British coercion (Intolerable/Coercive Acts, Boston Port Act) among the causes of the Revolution.

Standard Text: Compare and contrast the points of view of Loyalists and Patriots.
Cartoon Title: A Society of Patriotic Ladies, at Edenton in North Carolina
Creator: Attributed to Philip Dawe (London mezzotint)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Attributed to Philip Dawe, "A Society of Patriotic Ladies, at Edenton in North Carolina," 1775. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: British satirical mezzotint mocking American women signing a tea-boycott pledge at Edenton, ridiculing Patriot resistance.
Fit / Note: A Loyalist/British satire ridiculing Patriot activity — excellent for contrasting Loyalist and Patriot points of view.

Standard Text:
Locate and explain the significance of the following during the American Revolution:
• Struggles of the Continental Army
• Battles of Trenton and Princeton
• Battle of Kings Mountain
• Battle of Saratoga
• Battle of Yorktown
• Guerrilla warfare
Cartoon Title: The Horse America, throwing his Master
Creator: Unknown (London print)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Horse America, throwing his Master," 1779. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A rearing horse labeled 'America' throws off its British rider (King George III) who wields a whip and cudgel, symbolizing the colonies' military resistance.
Fit / Note: Satirizes Britain's inability to subdue America militarily during the war of independence.

Standard Text: Describe the conflict between Federalists and Anti-Federalists over the ratification of the Constitution, including the protection of individual rights through the Bill of Rights and concern for states’ rights. (T.C.A. § 49-6-1028)
Cartoon Title: The Federal Edifice (The Federal Pillars)
Creator: Massachusetts Centinel (Benjamin Russell)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Federal Edifice," Massachusetts Centinel, 1788. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A rising classical building supported by pillars, each labeled for a ratifying state, with a hand raising the next pillar into place.
Fit / Note: The famous ratification 'pillars' series tracking states joining the Union — ideal for the Federalist push for the Constitution.

Standard Text: Explain how conflicts between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton resulted in the emergence of two political parties by analyzing their views on foreign policy, economic policy, a national bank, and strict versus loose interpretation of the Constitution.
Cartoon Title: The Providential Detection
Creator: Unknown (Federalist print)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Providential Detection," c. 1797–1800. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: An American eagle stops Thomas Jefferson from burning the Constitution on an altar to French radicalism, satirizing the emerging party divide.
Fit / Note: A Federalist attack on Jefferson illustrating the partisan conflict that produced the first two political parties.

Standard Text: Explain the controversies that plagued the administration of President John Adams, including: the conflicts with Great Britain and France, the XYZ Affair, and the Alien and Sedition Acts.
Cartoon Title: Congressional Pugilists
Creator: Unknown (American engraving)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "Congressional Pugilists," 1798. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Congressmen Matthew Lyon and Roger Griswold brawl with cane and fire tongs on the floor of the House of Representatives.
Fit / Note: Captures the extreme Federalist–Republican partisanship of the Adams years surrounding the Alien and Sedition Acts.

Standard Text: Analyze the significance of the election of 1800 and Chief Justice John Marshall’s opinion in Marbury v. Madison.
Cartoon Title: Mad Tom in a Rage
Creator: Unknown (Federalist print)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "Mad Tom in a Rage," c. 1801. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Thomas Jefferson, aided by the devil, tries to pull down a pillar of the federal government, a Federalist attack tied to the election of 1800.
Fit / Note: A partisan reaction to Jefferson's victory in the 'Revolution of 1800.'

Standard Text:
Explain the major events of Thomas Jefferson’s presidency, including:
• Conflict with the Barbary pirates
• Embargo Act
• Lewis and Clark Expedition
• Louisiana Purchase
Cartoon Title: Ograbme, or The American Snapping Turtle (The Embargo)
Creator: Attributed to Alexander Anderson
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "Ograbme" (The Embargo), c. 1807. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A snapping turtle labeled 'Ograbme' (Embargo spelled backward) bites a merchant trying to smuggle goods to a British ship.
Fit / Note: The iconic protest cartoon against Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807.

Standard Text:
Explain the causes, course, and consequences of the War of 1812, including:
• Use of impressment and trade restrictions between the U.S. and Great Britain
• Roles of Andrew Jackson and William Henry Harrison
• Significance of the Treaty of Ghent
• Rise in nationalism in the U.S.
Cartoon Title: A Boxing Match, or Another Bloody Nose for John Bull
Creator: William Charles
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: William Charles, "A Boxing Match, or Another Bloody Nose for John Bull," 1813. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: President Madison and King George III as boxers; John Bull bleeds after a blow, celebrating a U.S. naval victory in the War of 1812.
Fit / Note: American War-of-1812 propaganda fueling the surge of postwar nationalism.

Standard Text: Analyze the characteristics of Southern society and its influence on the social and political conditions prior to the Civil War.
Cartoon Title: Slavery As It Exists in America
Creator: Unknown (American lithograph)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "Slavery As It Exists in America," 1850. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A pro-slavery cartoon contrasting an idealized scene of enslaved people in the American South with harsh Northern/British industrial labor.
Fit / Note: A Southern pro-slavery defense useful for analyzing how Southern society justified itself; teach as biased primary-source argument (author's purpose/point of view).

Standard Text: Identify the push-pull factors for Irish and German immigrants, and describe the impact of their arrival in the U.S. prior to the Civil War.
Cartoon Title: The Propagation Society, More Free than Welcome
Creator: Nathaniel Currier
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Nathaniel Currier, "The Propagation Society, More Free than Welcome," 1855. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A nativist cartoon showing the Pope and Catholic clergy landing in America, expressing fears about Irish and Catholic immigration.
Fit / Note: A Know-Nothing-era nativist cartoon reflecting reaction to Irish (Catholic) immigration before the Civil War; teach the anti-immigrant bias critically.

Standard Text: Analyze the development of the women’s suffrage movement, including the Seneca Falls Convention, and the ideals of Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Sojourner Truth.
Cartoon Title: The Age of Brass, or the Triumphs of Woman's Rights
Creator: Currier & Ives
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Currier & Ives, "The Age of Brass, or the Triumphs of Woman's Rights," 1869. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A satirical cartoon of women voting and asserting rights while a man minds a baby, mocking the woman-suffrage movement.
Fit / Note: An anti-suffrage satire useful for analyzing opposition to the women's-rights movement launched at Seneca Falls; teach the bias/point of view.

Standard Text: Analyze the significance of leading abolitionists, including William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass, Elihu Embree, and Harriet Tubman, and the methods they used to spread the movement.
Cartoon Title: Practical Illustration of the Fugitive Slave Law
Creator: Edward Williams Clay (attributed)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "Practical Illustration of the Fugitive Slave Law," 1851. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison defends a fugitive slave against a mounted slave catcher, dramatizing the abolition struggle.
Fit / Note: Prominently features named abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison confronting the slave-catching system.

Standard Text: Examine the importance of the elections of 1824 and 1828, including: the corrupt bargain, the spoils system, and Jacksonian Democracy.
Cartoon Title: A Foot-Race
Creator: David Claypoole Johnston
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: David Claypoole Johnston, "A Foot-Race," 1824. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Candidates Andrew Jackson, John Quincy Adams, and William Crawford race toward the presidency as onlookers wager on the 1824 election.
Fit / Note: Depicts the contested election of 1824 that produced the 'corrupt bargain.'

Standard Text: Examine President Andrew Jackson’s actions regarding the Bank of the U.S. and the Nullification Crisis, and analyze the effects of these events on the nation.
Cartoon Title: King Andrew the First
Creator: Unknown (anti-Jackson Whig print)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "King Andrew the First," c. 1833. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Andrew Jackson stands as a crowned king in royal robes, trampling the Constitution and holding a veto, after vetoing the Bank of the United States.
Fit / Note: The definitive Bank War cartoon attacking Jackson's veto and expansion of executive power.

Unit / Cluster: Expansion and Division of the Nation (1820s-1860s)
Standard Text: Analyze the discovery of gold in California, its social and economic impact on the U.S., and the major migratory movement (including the forty-niners and Asian immigrants).
Cartoon Title: The Way They Go to California
Creator: Nathaniel Currier (Currier & Ives)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Nathaniel Currier, "The Way They Go to California," 1849. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Crowds of fortune-seekers scramble aboard overloaded ships and fanciful flying machines bound for the California gold fields.
Fit / Note: Satirizes the frenzy of the 1849 Gold Rush and the mass migration west.

Unit / Cluster: Expansion and Division of the Nation (1820s-1860s)
Standard Text: Explain the reasons for and the impact of the Compromise of 1850 (including Henry Clay’s role as “The Great Compromiser”) and the Fugitive Slave Act (including Harriet Beecher Stowe’s influence with Uncle Tom’s Cabin).
Cartoon Title: Effects of the Fugitive-Slave-Law
Creator: Theodor Kaufmann (lithograph, Hoff & Bloede)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Theodor Kaufmann, "Effects of the Fugitive-Slave-Law," 1850. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Armed slave catchers ambush and fire on a group of Black men in a field, condemning the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
Fit / Note: A Northern indictment of the Fugitive Slave Act, a core provision of the Compromise of 1850.

Unit / Cluster: Expansion and Division of the Nation (1820s-1860s)
Standard Text:
Explain the motivations behind the passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and analyze the effects of act, including:
• Rise of the Republican Party
• “Bleeding Kansas”
• Preston Brooks’ attack on Charles Sumner
• John Brown’s raid at Harper’s Ferry
Cartoon Title: Forcing Slavery Down the Throat of a Freesoiler
Creator: John L. Magee
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: John L. Magee, "Forcing Slavery Down the Throat of a Freesoiler," 1856. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Democratic leaders (Douglas, Pierce, Buchanan, Cass) hold down a giant Free-Soiler on the Democratic platform and force slavery into his mouth, over a burning Kansas.
Fit / Note: The signature cartoon of 'Bleeding Kansas' and the Kansas-Nebraska crisis; task-named.

Standard Text: Describe the election of 1860 and its candidates (i.e., John Bell, Stephen Douglas, Abraham Lincoln, and John Breckinridge), and analyze how the campaigns reflected sectional turmoil in the country.
Cartoon Title: The Political Quadrille, Music by Dred Scott
Creator: Unknown (American lithograph)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Political Quadrille, Music by Dred Scott," 1860. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: The four 1860 presidential candidates each dance with a partner while Dred Scott plays the fiddle at the center, mocking the fractured campaign.
Fit / Note: Depicts all four candidates (Lincoln, Douglas, Breckinridge, Bell) of the four-way 1860 race and its sectional turmoil.

Standard Text:
Describe the outbreak of the Civil War and the resulting sectional differences, including:
• Economic, geographic, and technological advances
• Military strategies
• Roles of President Abraham Lincoln and Jefferson Davis
• Significance of Fort Sumter
• Geographical divisions within states
Cartoon Title: Scott's Great Snake (The Anaconda Plan)
Creator: J. B. Elliott of Cincinnati
Repository: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
Academic Citation: J. B. Elliott, "Scott's Great Snake," Cincinnati, 1861. Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A cartoon map showing a giant snake labeled 'Scott' coiling around the Southern states and blockading the coast and Mississippi River.
Fit / Note: A cartoon map illustrating Winfield Scott's Anaconda Plan — Union military strategy at the outbreak of war.

Standard Text: Analyze the significance of the Emancipation Proclamation and the Gettysburg Address.
Cartoon Title: Emancipation
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "Emancipation," King & Baird / Harper's Weekly, 1863–1865. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: Thomas Nast's allegory contrasting the horrors of slavery with a hopeful future of freedom for African Americans after emancipation.
Fit / Note: Nast's celebrated visual argument for the meaning of the Emancipation Proclamation.

Standard Text: Explain the significance of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the U.S. Constitution.
Cartoon Title: And Not This Man?
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: HarpWeek / Harper's Weekly (via Library of Congress)
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "Franchise. And Not This Man?" Harper's Weekly, August 5, 1865. Public domain.
Alt Text: Columbia points to a wounded Black Union veteran on crutches and asks whether he should be denied the vote, arguing for Black suffrage.
Fit / Note: Nast's argument for the voting rights secured by the 14th and 15th Amendments.

Standard Text: Analyze the conflict between President Andrew Johnson and the Radical Republicans, including Johnson’s veto of the Tenure of Office Act and his impeachment.
Cartoon Title: Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction and How It Works
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: HarpWeek / Harper's Weekly (via Library of Congress)
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction and How It Works," Harper's Weekly, September 1, 1866. Public domain.
Alt Text: President Andrew Johnson portrayed as Iago beside a wounded Black veteran, blaming Johnson's lenient Reconstruction for postwar violence.
Fit / Note: Nast's attack on Johnson dramatizes the clash between the president and the Radical Republicans that led to impeachment.

Standard Text: Explain the restrictions placed on the rights and opportunities of freedmen, including: racial segregation, black codes, and the efforts of the Freedmen's Bureau to address the problems confronting newly freed slaves.
Cartoon Title: The Freedman's Bureau! An Agency to Keep the Negro in Idleness
Creator: Unknown (Pennsylvania Democratic campaign broadside)
Repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
Academic Citation: "The Freedman's Bureau!" campaign broadside, Pennsylvania, 1866. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Public domain.
Alt Text: A racist 1866 campaign cartoon caricaturing a Black man lounging while attacking the Freedmen's Bureau as wasteful to white taxpayers.
Fit / Note: A racist anti-Freedmen's-Bureau campaign cartoon; teach critically as evidence of white political opposition to freedmen's rights and the bias of the source.

Standard Text: Trace the rise of the Ku Klux Klan and vigilante justice in the South and in Tennessee, including the role of Governor William Brownlow.
Cartoon Title: This Is a White Man's Government
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: HarpWeek / Harper's Weekly (via Library of Congress)
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "This Is a White Man's Government," Harper's Weekly, September 5, 1868. Public domain.
Alt Text: An Irish rioter, a Ku Klux Klan member, and a Confederate (Nathan Bedford Forrest) clasp hands while trampling a Black Union veteran reaching for a ballot box.
Fit / Note: Nast condemns the Klan and vigilante suppression of Black voters; the Confederate figure is Tennessee's Nathan Bedford Forrest; task-named.

Standard Text: Explain the roles carpetbaggers and scalawags played during Reconstruction.
Cartoon Title: The Man with the (Carpet) Bags
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: HarpWeek / Harper's Weekly (via Library of Congress)
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "The Man with the (Carpet) Bags," Harper's Weekly, 1872. Public domain.
Alt Text: A traveler loaded down with carpetbags, satirizing the 'carpetbagger' figure of Reconstruction politics.
Fit / Note: Directly illustrates the 'carpetbagger' epithet central to this standard on carpetbaggers and scalawags.

Standard Text: Explain the Compromise of 1877 and its role in ending Radical Reconstruction.
Cartoon Title: A Truce — Not a Compromise
Creator: Thomas Nast
Repository: HarpWeek / Harper's Weekly (via Library of Congress)
Academic Citation: Thomas Nast, "A Truce — Not a Compromise," Harper's Weekly, 1877. Public domain.
Alt Text: A Union and a Confederate figure warily shake hands over a divide, commenting on the disputed 1876 election settlement.
Fit / Note: Nast's commentary on the Compromise of 1877 that ended Radical Reconstruction.
